weather-inside-your-calendar.title: A calendar with the weather already in it
weather-inside-your-calendar.description: Why checking two apps to plan one day is a design failure, and what a calendar looks like when the forecast is part of it rather than beside it.
weather-inside-your-calendar.lede: Almost everyone plans a day across two apps. The calendar says where you have to be; the weather app says what it will be like when you get there. Holding both in your head is the part nobody notices they are doing, until a Saturday gets rained on.
weather-inside-your-calendar.commonBelief: That a calendar is for commitments and a weather app is for weather, and keeping them separate is simply how phones work.

sections.heading: The cost of two apps is not two taps
body: The tax is not the switching. It is that the two apps disagree about what matters. Your calendar knows Saturday has a two-hour block at eleven; your weather app knows it will rain from ten until one. Neither of them knows that those two facts, together, mean you should move the block.
You are the integration layer. That works until you are busy, which is exactly when plans are worth protecting.

sections.heading: Match the forecast to the plan
body: Use the available hourly and daily forecasts for the selected location alongside your schedule. Check that the dates and hours you need are actually present; a daily summary does not establish hourly coverage for every event.

Calendar navigation reaches beyond weather data. A month or year view does not promise conditions for every date displayed. If your plan lies outside the available forecast, keep the calendar entry and check the weather closer to its date.

sections.heading: What the app’s forecast range means
body: Cloud Calendars uses Apple WeatherKit. The inspected native code requests daily data and limits its daily list to at most ten returned entries. A list can contain fewer entries; this is not a guarantee of complete data for every location or future event.
The website’s weather demonstration is separate from the native app. Its range is not evidence that the app provides fourteen days of forecasts.

claims.price: Cost of the weather features, in pounds, dollars or euros

practical: Confirm the selected location and the forecast date.
Compare the available hours with the hours of your plan.
If the event is beyond the available forecast, check again nearer the date.

forecast-beside-every-event.title: The forecast beside every event, not just the day
forecast-beside-every-event.description: A daily summary averages away the hours you care about. What per-event weather looks like, and why the difference matters for anything scheduled outdoors.
forecast-beside-every-event.lede: Most calendars that mention weather show one icon per day. That icon is an average, and an average of a wet morning and a dry afternoon is a drizzle that never happens.
forecast-beside-every-event.commonBelief: That a daily weather icon on a calendar is the same feature as a forecast attached to an event.

sections.heading: What a daily icon hides
body: Take a day that rains hard until eleven and stays clear afterwards. The daily summary picks something in the middle and shows a cloud. You look at your two o'clock, see the cloud, and move a walk that never needed moving.
The error runs both ways. A day that is fine except for a violent hour at six shows as fine, and the one event that mattered is the one that gets caught.

sections.heading: Attaching the forecast to the hours
body: An event occupies specific hours. The forecast for those hours is a different number from the forecast for its day, and it is the only one that answers the question you are actually asking.
Open an event and the conditions shown are the ones for its window. A three-hour block gets the three hours, not the twenty-four.

practical: Check the event, not the day, whenever the plan depends on the weather.
For anything longer than a couple of hours, look at how the conditions move across the block rather than at a single figure.
Move the event before you cancel it — an hour either way is often the whole difference.

a-fourteen-day-view-of-the-weather.title: How far ahead does the available forecast reach?
a-fourteen-day-view-of-the-weather.description: Check the dates a forecast actually covers. Calendar navigation, daily forecasts and hourly detail are different ranges in Cloud Calendars.
a-fourteen-day-view-of-the-weather.lede: You can create an appointment far beyond the dates covered by weather data. That does not make the forecast reach the appointment. Check the available dates before using weather to choose a time.
a-fourteen-day-view-of-the-weather.commonBelief: Every future date visible in a calendar has a matching weather forecast.

sections.heading: Separate the calendar range from the forecast range
body: A calendar can hold a plan for next month without knowing next month’s weather. Look at the forecast dates themselves, rather than the month you can open in the calendar. No weather entry for a date should be treated as missing information, not as a prediction of clear conditions.

sections.heading: What the native app requests
body: Apple describes WeatherKit as providing ten-day hourly forecasts. In the inspected Cloud Calendars source, the daily list uses at most ten entries returned by WeatherKit. That supports removing the old fourteen-day promise; it does not establish that every request or location will return a complete ten days.
The homepage demonstration and the native app use separate weather implementations. A range offered by the demonstration is not a promise about the app.

sections.heading: Check the detail you actually need
body: Confirm the selected place, date and hours. Daily and hourly displays need not expose identical ranges. Do not assume a daily forecast contains every hour of a long event.

For a plan beyond the available dates, choose a tentative date based on your calendar and revisit the forecast later. Forecast information can change; this article does not assign a universal confidence threshold to a particular day.

practical: Read the first and last dates actually available.
Check hourly coverage separately from the daily list.
Keep future plans provisional when weather information is not available.

planning-outdoors-without-being-rained-o.title: Planning outdoor things without getting rained on
planning-outdoors-without-being-rained-o.description: A practical method for scheduling anything that happens outside, using the calendar you already keep rather than a separate weather routine.
planning-outdoors-without-being-rained-o.lede: If your hobbies happen outdoors you have probably built a private ritual: check the weather, squint at the week, guess. The guessing is the part that can go.
planning-outdoors-without-being-rained-o.commonBelief: That avoiding bad weather means checking the forecast more often.

sections.heading: Checking more is not the answer
body: Opening a weather app five times does not improve the forecast; it improves your anxiety. What changes outcomes is looking at the forecast at the moment you are choosing a time, which is a different moment entirely.
That moment happens in the calendar. If the weather is not there, you are making the decision without it and correcting later.

sections.heading: Choose the slot against the week
body: Look at the week with the conditions behind it and the choice usually makes itself. Two candidate afternoons, one dry — there is nothing to deliberate about.
The habit worth building is small: before you place anything outdoors, look at the band, not at a separate app.

sections.heading: Then check the hours, not the day
body: Once the event exists, its own forecast is the one that matters. A day can be wet and your two hours dry, and the daily summary will never tell you that.
Move before you cancel. An hour in either direction rescues more plans than any amount of re-checking.

practical: Place outdoor events from the week view, with conditions visible.
Two days out, check the event's own hours rather than its day.
Shift by an hour before abandoning the plan.
For anything more than a week away, pick the day and accept you will refine it later.

what-a-forecast-can-and-cannot-tell-you.title: What a forecast can and cannot tell you
what-a-forecast-can-and-cannot-tell-you.short: What a forecast can tell you
what-a-forecast-can-and-cannot-tell-you.description: Forecasts are probabilistic, and reading them as promises is why they feel unreliable. A short guide to what the numbers actually mean.
what-a-forecast-can-and-cannot-tell-you.lede: Weather forecasts are not wrong nearly as often as they feel wrong. Most of the gap is a mismatch between what they say and what people hear.
what-a-forecast-can-and-cannot-tell-you.commonBelief: That a forecast is a statement about what will happen.

sections.heading: It is a distribution, not a plan
body: A forecast is the output of many model runs that disagree with each other. What you are shown is roughly where they cluster. When they cluster tightly, the forecast is confident; when they scatter, it is not — and the icon looks the same either way.
This is why two forecasts that were both 'right' can feel different: one had no real competition, the other was a coin toss that landed.

sections.heading: Where it is strong
body: Temperature is reliable further out than precipitation. Whether tomorrow is warm is a much easier question than whether it rains at four, and the difference is not small.
Timing of a front is usually better than intensity. You can often trust that rain arrives in the afternoon while not trusting how much falls.

sections.heading: Where it is weak
body: Anything convective — summer thunderstorms, sharp showers — is guesswork about placement. The model may be certain that storms happen in the region and unable to say whether one crosses your park.
Mountains, coasts and cities all bend the local picture in ways a grid forecast smooths away.

practical: Trust temperature further out than rain.
Treat a chance of showers as a chance, not a schedule.
For convective weather, check again on the morning; nothing earlier will settle it.
If a plan cannot survive being wrong, build the fallback rather than refreshing the forecast.

reading-a-chance-of-rain.title: What a forty per cent chance of rain actually means
reading-a-chance-of-rain.description: The single most misread number in any forecast, explained — and what to do with it when you are deciding whether to move an event.
reading-a-chance-of-rain.lede: Almost nobody reads probability of precipitation the way it is meant. The number is not how much rain, and it is not how long.
reading-a-chance-of-rain.commonBelief: That forty per cent means light rain, or rain for part of the day.

sections.heading: What the number is
body: It is the probability that measurable rain falls at a given point in the forecast area during the period. Forty per cent means: in four out of ten runs of this situation, the spot you are standing on gets wet.
It says nothing about how hard, and nothing about for how long. A forty per cent day can be a five-minute shower or an afternoon of it.

sections.heading: Why it feels wrong so often
body: Because people grade it as a yes or a no. Stay dry on a forty per cent day and the forecast 'was wrong'; get soaked and it 'was right'. Neither is true — the number was a bet, and bets lose six times in ten.
Over a season a well-calibrated forty per cent rains about forty per cent of the time, which is exactly the point and is invisible from any single day.

practical: Read it as odds, not as intensity.
Under about thirty per cent, plan normally and carry a contingency.
Above about sixty, plan for rain and be pleasantly surprised.
Between the two, look at the hours rather than the day — that is where the answer usually is.

weather-where-the-event-is.title: The weather where the event is, not where you are
weather-where-the-event-is.description: Your phone knows where you are. Your event knows where it is going to be. For anything more than a few miles away, those are different forecasts.
weather-where-the-event-is.lede: A forecast pinned to your current location is the right answer for right now and the wrong answer for a match forty miles away.
weather-where-the-event-is.commonBelief: That one local forecast covers everything in your day.

sections.heading: Distance changes the answer faster than people expect
body: Rain bands are not uniform. Twenty miles inland can be dry while the coast is not; a valley and the ridge above it disagree routinely. For a commute this is noise. For a fixture, a hike or a site visit it is the whole question.
The event carries a place. Using it is simply using information you already gave the calendar.

sections.heading: What this fixes in practice
body: The classic failure is packing for home weather and arriving somewhere else. It is not a forecasting error at all — the forecast was right about the wrong place.
When an event has a location, its conditions should follow the location rather than the phone.

practical: Put a real location on events that happen somewhere else.
For travel days, check the destination rather than the origin.
If the location is vague, the forecast is vague too — a postcode beats a place name.

the-commute-and-the-sky.title: The two half-hours of your day that the weather actually ruins
the-commute-and-the-sky.description: Most weather disruption is not the day, it is the two commutes. A small habit that catches nearly all of it.
the-commute-and-the-sky.lede: Ask people when weather last inconvenienced them and they will mostly describe a journey, not an afternoon.
the-commute-and-the-sky.commonBelief: That a wet day is a wet day, and there is nothing to be done about it.

sections.heading: The exposure is narrow
body: For most people the genuinely weather-exposed part of a working day is two short journeys. Everything between them happens indoors.
That makes the problem far smaller than it feels, and far more tractable: you are not trying to predict a day, only two half-hours.

sections.heading: Which changes what you check
body: The useful question is not whether it rains today but whether it rains at eight and at six. Those are two specific hours, and hourly detail answers them well inside the range where forecasts are strong.
Shifting a departure by twenty minutes is often the entire fix, and it is only visible if you looked at the hours.

practical: Check the two commute hours rather than the day.
Twenty minutes earlier or later is usually enough to miss a shower.
If both ends look wet, that is the day to take the bag rather than the bike.

daylight-as-a-planning-constraint.title: Daylight is a constraint, and calendars usually ignore it
daylight-as-a-planning-constraint.description: Sunset moves by minutes a day and by hours across a season. For anything outdoors it binds harder than the weather does.
daylight-as-a-planning-constraint.lede: Weather is uncertain. Daylight is not, and yet most plans are made as though only the first one existed.
daylight-as-a-planning-constraint.commonBelief: That the light will hold because it held last week.

sections.heading: The number moves faster than intuition
body: Around the equinoxes sunset shifts by two to three minutes a day at mid-latitudes. Over a fortnight that is half an hour, which is the difference between finishing in light and finishing by phone torch.
In late autumn the change is sharpest exactly when people are still scheduling as though it were September.

sections.heading: Use it as a hard edge
body: Unlike rain, sunset is certain. It is the one planning input that never surprises you, and it deserves to be treated as a wall rather than a suggestion.
Work backwards from it: a two-hour activity that must finish in daylight has a latest start, and that start moves every week.

practical: Work backwards from sunset for anything outdoors, not forwards from the free slot.
Re-check the latest safe start every couple of weeks in spring and autumn.
In the fortnight after the clocks change, assume your instincts are an hour wrong.

wind-the-forecast-nobody-reads.title: Wind is the forecast nobody reads and half of them needed
wind-the-forecast-nobody-reads.description: Cycling, sailing, paddling, drone flying, gardening, anything with a gazebo. For a lot of plans wind decides the day and rain does not.
wind-the-forecast-nobody-reads.lede: People check rain out of habit. For a surprising number of activities, wind is the number that actually determines whether the thing happens.
wind-the-forecast-nobody-reads.commonBelief: That wind is a detail and rain is the headline.

sections.heading: Where wind is the binding constraint
body: A dry day at thirty knots cancels more plans than a damp one at five. Cyclists, sailors, paddlers, anyone putting up a marquee, anyone flying anything — for all of them the rain line is secondary.
It is also the number people are worst at estimating from a window, because a sheltered street tells you very little about an exposed route.

sections.heading: Direction matters as much as speed
body: The same speed is a different day depending on where it comes from. An offshore wind flattens water and pushes you out; onshore does the opposite. A headwind out is a tailwind home, which changes how far you plan to go.
Gust figures matter more than averages for anything with a sail or a canopy: the average holds the tent up, the gust takes it away.

practical: For wind-sensitive plans, check speed and direction, not just the icon.
Read the gusts, not the mean, for anything that can be lifted.
Plan the outbound leg into the wind so the tired leg is the easy one.

faq.lead: Still stuck? Everything about data handling is written out in the {link}.

items.q: Do I need an account to use Cloud Calendars?
items.a: Use local calendars without an account. Connecting calendar services and sharing may require sign-in.

items.q: Is Google Calendar sync really free?
items.a: Google Calendar and Google Meet support are included in Free. Advanced removes ads; Premium adds Microsoft Calendar and Teams.

items.q: Where does the weather data come from?
items.a: Forecasts are fetched for your current or chosen location and cover hourly and ten-day outlooks, feels-like temperature, precipitation, UV, wind and gusts, humidity and dew point, visibility, pressure, sunrise and sunset, and moon phase.

items.q: Can I change an event by dragging it?
items.a: That is the main way to edit. Drag an event to another time or another day, or pull its top or bottom edge to change the duration. Changes sync straight back to the source calendar.

Small and medium layouts show date and weather. Medium and large event lists show future timed appointments; find all-day entries in the app. Use Live Activity on supported devices. Updates may take time; check the app after a schedule change.

items.q: How do I cancel a subscription?
items.a: Subscriptions are handled by Apple, so you cancel in your App Store account settings. Do it at least 24 hours before the period ends and you will not be charged again.
